A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study of adversarial robustness and attack transfer in transformers learning linear regression. Despite the changed title and organization, the main text, figures, tables, equations, and Appendices A–C support a complete comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original synthetic-data experiments on hijacking attacks, adversarial training, model scaling, and transfer between transformers and ordinary least squares, including Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experimental results in its main text and Appendix B. They qualify independently of their appearance in v1.

M1.justification: The transformer architectures, constructive attacks, gradient-based attacks, and adversarial pretraining and finetuning procedures remain the same. Renaming x-, y-, and z-attacks as feature-, label-, and joint-attacks does not change their operations.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate the same synthetic Gaussian linear-regression tasks and adversarial scenarios. The added discussion of vision, tabular data, robotics, and clinical applications does not introduce evaluations in those domains.

E2.justification: Corresponding experiments retain the same linear transformer, GPT-2 depth variants, ordinary least squares solver, and training-condition comparators. This includes v1 Figure 1 versus v2 Figure 6, v1 Figure 6 versus v2 Figure 5, and the retained OLS comparisons.

E3.justification: The stated metrics, model configurations, training budgets, and attack-optimization settings are retained, including Tables 1–3 and Appendix C. v2 supplies previously missing curriculum, target-generation, and context-length details without establishing that the experimental protocols changed.

E4.justification: The depth and context-length analyses, attack-target interpolation experiments, attack-budget comparisons, accuracy–robustness analysis, and transfer studies are retained. Appendix B contains the same analyses; reorganizing their presentation adds no new ablation or robustness test.

E5.justification: v2 Section 5.1 newly specifies that the cross-depth transfer heatmap uses one randomly selected source and target model for each depth combination. Figure 4 also explicitly identifies its existing shading as standard error. These refine reporting; the PDFs do not establish additional runs or changed uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: Matched result plots throughout the main text and Appendix B retain identical curves, heatmap entries, and uncertainty bands. The robustness, adversarial-training, scaling, and transfer findings are unchanged; figure relocation and renumbering introduce no new results.

T1.justification: Theorem 4.1 and Appendix A retain the same assumptions, conclusions, derivation, and adversarial constructions. v2 explicitly spells out argument dependencies and matrix-block notation, clarifying the existing mathematics rather than adding or substantively revising a result.

C1.justification: The principal robustness and transfer findings remain. v2 adds explicit novelty claims about providing the first evidence that identically configured transformers may learn distinct algorithms and the first mechanistic explanation of hijacking vulnerability, sharpening the claimed contributions.

C2.justification: New Section 6.1 explains that transfer failure cannot distinguish different parameterizations of one algorithm from genuinely different algorithms, and limits extrapolation beyond simple linear regression. v2 also newly interprets successful adversarial training as suggesting an ability to solve challenging nonconvex optimization problems in context.

D1.justification: v2 documents Gram–Schmidt construction and normalization of the attack-target weight vector. Appendix C.2 completes the previously unfinished curriculum description: dimensions increase from 5 to 20 by one every 5,000 steps. Appendix C.3 also corrects the target-label expression to agree with v1's main text.

R1.justification: v2 adds references motivating applications in vision, tabular prediction, robotics, and medicine, plus Diakonikolas and Kane (2019), while pruning broader robustness and mesa-optimization references. It more explicitly positions transfer findings as challenging gradient-descent and OLS explanations, within the same research area.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and discussion are extensively rewritten. Robustness results are consolidated into Section 4, transfer studies are regrouped into Section 5, limitations and future-work subsections are added, and attack terminology changes throughout.

P2.justification: v2 adopts journal formatting and relocates or resizes retained figures, while updating captions and attack labels. Figure 4 changes its two panels from stacked to side-by-side. The plots and table structures remain substantially intact.

improvement.justification: Completing the training curriculum in Appendix C.2 and adding substantive limitations in Section 6.1 improve reproducibility and qualify the interpretation of transfer failures. The reorganized narrative also clarifies the two research questions. These are useful but limited gains: the theory and empirical evidence are unchanged, and the stronger algorithmic framing still rests on indirect evidence.
